entries.summary: The 24 Tirthankaras of the current cosmic cycle, in order: 1. Rishabhanatha (Adinatha), 2. Ajitanatha, 3. Sambhavanatha, 4. Abhinandananatha, 5. Sumatinatha, 6. Padmaprabha, 7. Suparshvanatha, 8. Chandraprabha, 9. Pushpadanta (Suvidhinatha), 10. Shitalanatha, 11. Shreyansanatha, 12. Vasupujya, 13. Vimalanatha, 14. Anantanatha, 15. Dharmanatha, 16. Shantinatha, 17. Kunthunatha, 18. Aranatha, 19. Mallinatha, 20. Munisuvratanatha, 21. Naminatha, 22. Neminatha (Arishtanemi), 23. Parshvanatha, 24. Mahavira (Vardhamana).
entries.tradition_notes: Both Digambara and Śvētāmbara agree on the list of 24 Tirthankaras. One notable difference: Śvētāmbara tradition considers the 19th Tirthankara Mallinatha to be female; Digambara tradition considers Mallinatha to be male.

entries.summary: Rishabhanatha, also known as Adinatha ('First Lord'), is the first Tirthankara of the current cosmic cycle. He is traditionally credited with teaching humans the arts of civilization — agriculture, pottery, commerce — as well as the path of renunciation. He is revered as the founder of Jainism in the current era. His son Bharata became the first Chakravarti (universal emperor), after whom India is traditionally said to be named (Bharatavarsha). Rishabhanatha is also mentioned in Hindu texts (Bhagavata Purana), reflecting his ancient cultural significance.
entries.tradition_notes: Revered by both Digambara and Śvētāmbara. Iconographically depicted with a bull emblem (lanchhan).

entries.summary: Parshvanatha is traditionally the 23rd Tirthankara, believed to have lived roughly 250 years before Mahavira (around the 9th–8th century BCE by traditional reckoning). He is historically significant: many scholars consider him the earliest Tirthankara for whom there is meaningful historical evidence distinct from legendary accounts. He is associated with a fourfold vow of non-violence, truth, non-stealing, and non-possessiveness (Mahavira later added celibacy as the fifth). Parshvanatha is often depicted in Jain art with a multi-headed serpent canopy above him.
entries.tradition_notes: Revered by both traditions. His four-vow system vs. Mahavira's five vows is a discussed topic in Jain history.

entries.summary: Neminatha, also known as Arishtanemi, is the 22nd Tirthankara. Jain tradition holds that he was a cousin of Krishna (of the Mahabharata). He is said to have renounced worldly life on his wedding day after witnessing animals being slaughtered for the feast, moved by compassion. He is venerated especially in Gujarat and Rajasthan. His story emphasizes ahimsa and the turning away from worldly pleasures.
entries.tradition_notes: Revered by both traditions. His connection to Krishna is accepted in Jain texts.

entries.summary: Mallinatha is the 19th Tirthankara and is notable for a key difference between the two major Jain traditions: Śvētāmbara tradition holds that Mallinatha was female (Mali), making her the only female Tirthankara. Digambara tradition holds that Mallinatha was male. The Śvētāmbara text Nayadhammakahao contains the story of Malli's life.
entries.tradition_notes: This is one of the well-known doctrinal differences between Digambara and Śvētāmbara traditions. The Digambara position is that a woman cannot attain Kevala Jnana and hence Tirthankara status in a female body. Śvētāmbara disagrees.
